Automated agentic emailing vs the real world, a story:
Guy emails me twice to meet at a conference (Slush)
I reply once
He then emails me 3 times in rapid succession
Damn that guy really wants to meet
I bump into him later that day
I say “well, was meant to be”
He reads my name tag, twice.
Blank face. He clearly has no idea who I am.
He says “oh hi” and walks away.
The end.

item.description:
作者：Aaron Levie 账号：@levie 简介：ceo @box - your business lives in content. unleash it with AI
This year we’ve had a clear jump in model capability where instead of telling agents precisely what to do, it’s better to use these systems to solve problems you can’t easily define yourself.
A year ago you’d need to very clearly tell agents the how to design and develop your product idea, or there was almost no chance of success. Now, increasingly, the agent likely can come up with a better implementation than you’d have thought of because you can have it connect the dots between a far greater solution space than you can.
This will be increasingly true in basically every domain of kneeler work. We’re going to see this impact in finance, legal, life sciences, cyber, and many other spaces where no person can hold onto all the available relevant industry knowledge to think of the best solution.
Ultimately this is going to reshape our relationship with AI and how we deploy agents in our work. It won’t be about explicitly telling them, but instead giving them goals and enough freedom to pursue them in the best way they can.

item.title: Scaling Linear’s GTM to $100M ARR — Cristina Cordova, COO
item.description:
播客：Latent Space
Kari writing this blog post, like issue tracking is dead. Yeah.
So like how do you explain to your customers that like, "Hey, you know, our entire business was issue tracking before, and now our CEO just wrote this blog post"?
The great thing about our business is that we're not like so big to like kill ourselves, right? [laughs] Yeah. Like [laughs] um- [laughs]...
it's probably really hard if you're Google to like kill the search business, right? Yeah. And put an AI, you know, box at the top of every search result, and maybe no one's gonna look at the ads, right?
So your entire business is upended. And like yes, the unit of the issue still exists, but we probably shouldn't have a world where people are like manually tracking work. Yeah. So like that's what's dead, right?
So in a lot of cases when we were talking to various customers as this, you know, blog post came out, most of our customers were like, "Yeah." [laughs] "Issue tracking is dead. And by the way, like, what are you guys?
What am I buying?" [laughs] Right? [upbeat music] Christina Cordova, you're the COO of Linear. Could you introduce yourself? Yeah, yeah. So I'm Christina.
Um, I've been at Linear for about three and a half years now, joined as COO, and I'm still COO today.
Prior to Linear, I spent time at Notion leading our platform, so the build-out of our APIs, and then our partnerships and self-serve growth initiatives as well.
And then before that, I was at Stripe for seven and a half years, and there I led a lot of our early partnerships and go-to-market, um, and then moved over to the product side and built out some new products for early-stage companies.
So I've been probably anywhere from like the product side of a company and like managing engineers all the way to, uh, managing, you know, the business side of a company as well, um, which has been really fun.
So why did Linear hire a COO at like 40 employees? Is that like odd- [laughs]... or is that pretty normal? Um, I mean, I, I generally don't believe every company needs a COO. Yeah. Right?
Like when I talk to founders and they're like, "Hey, like I think I've found product market fit. Like how do we start to scale like the business side of the company?"
I am often I feel like cautioning against maybe hiring someone like me. [laughs] Yeah. So I think for every company it's a little bit different.
I think you have to really understand as like a founder, like what are the things you need and what are the things you're looking for in the people that you bring onto the team?
Often early on it's just like I need someone to like sell something, right? [laughs] Uh, we have expanded beyond the capability of the founder or CEO to sell every net new customer, right?
So there I generally talk about, well, you should hire folks in sales, maybe hire a sales leader- Yeah... to build out a team, right?
But if you're not exactly sure what you're looking for in like marketing or operations or other parts of the company, um, then it may very well not make sense to hire someone like me.
You know, I think with the Linear founders, um, you know, they were incredibly focused on like design and engineering and product, um, and I think they had a really great, you know, kind of combination of skills between the three of them.
But as we were starting to scale the business side of the company, they didn't necessarily look at like the next salesperson that we hired and said, "Hmm, I know exactly what we're looking for here, and I know whether or not sales is performing really well," right?
So if you don't look at different parts of your company and say like, "Okay, I know what great is, and I feel like I have a good sense of like how to get to great," it can sometimes be helpful to hire someone like me or like a functional leader, like when it comes time to do that.
Yeah, so like what did the business look like at that point? Like can you talk about like what revenue they were at or... Yeah, we were probably,
I wanna say, you know, we had some large customers but no like public company customers. Yeah. Uh, probably no customer above, I wanna say, like maybe 500 seats or something like that.
So I would say like m- we mostly tapped out at like mid-market, and we were probably best well known for being a great product for startups, but not necessarily a great product for other companies- Yeah... at that time.
Um, you know, and I think at that point in time, we were, we're doing well with like a product-led growth model- Mm... where most people were using our product because they signed up self-serve. Mm.
Um, and then grew with us over time. So companies like Vercel and Ramp and many other customers like that, you know, really never talked to a human being, um, at Linear.
Signed up for the product, started using it, and then started scaling, which was great. Like you know the product can do a lot of work on its own. Yeah.
But it was also star- like time to start selling to, you know, the company that is not even gonna put like a lick of data into your service without, you know, signing a contract- Yeah...
and doing a pilot and, uh, surveying their team on, you know, what tool they were using before and what to, you know, what tool is this and what's better, right?
Um, so that was a very different kind of motion for the company to start scaling to larger, uh, companies, and that was like pretty much my objective. Um, and we've at least 10Xed, I think, since I joined. Nice. So.
And you joined like four years ago? Uh, three, almost three and a half years ago, yeah. Oh, okay. So I think the Linear founders have talked about this.
I think you have as well, that like w- before you join Linear you always do a, like a trial period. Yes. So did you also have to do- Yes... a trial period? I did. Okay. Yeah, yeah. So yeah, like what was that like?
Yeah, I mean, I think my project was quite simple. It was something like, uh, you know, come up with the go-to-market plan for Linear, you know, with a bounded time period, like for the next six to 12 months- Yeah...
or something like that, right? And I think the good thing about that is that, you know, that is the job, [laughs] like right? Yeah.
So you're not giving someone some like fictional project that's not really like representative of like what they would do when they join the company.
It's like a real, uh, project, and that would, you know, effectively be my job in joining the company. So- Yeah... you know, if they didn't like the outcomes that I produced- [laughs]...
as part of that project, they probably, you know, shouldn't hire me. Yeah.
Um, so I think it was a really good way of saying like, "I have some ideas of what the company can do better, but also I wanna like get feedback from the people who are on the ground."
Like, you know, we had a salesperson on our team. We had someone doing customer success. Uh, we had some people doing support, and, you know, one or two folks doing marketing, right?
Um, so kind of getting their perspectives on different parts of the business and, like, where I should focus and where to, where to prioritize, and then making sure that, like, the company was also bought in on, like, that vision for the world, uh, was, I think, really helpful for me.
And then when I actually started at the company, it was almost like I had this little blueprint- Yeah... for, you know, what my job should be and what I should accomplish. Can you talk about, like, what was in that plan?
[laughs] Um, I think a, a lot of it was, like, brand and marketing oriented, so like, you know, things around, like, making Linear inevitable, um, in a lot of ways.
So, you know, either you're already on Linear, or you should be, like, planning your move to Linear [laughs] effectively. Yeah.
Um, and most companies that we want to acquire should be, you know, in, you know, one world or the other.
So a lot of that was around, you know, driving the brand, building storytelling...
